name: Old Persian
confidence_why: Kent 1950, Meillet 1915, Meillet and Benveniste 1931 and Schmitt 2004 all state that the Old Persian cuneiform inscriptions give no evidence for the place or nature of the accent beyond the existence of enclitics, and Skjaervo 2016 offers only a hedged comparative reconstruction (stress on the rightmost non-final heavy syllable) while saying outright that the rules are not known, so the classification that Old Persian stress is undetermined is the clear consensus.

tone_statements.citation: Meillet, Antoine. 1900. La déclinaison et l'accent d'intensité en perse. Journal Asiatique, 9e série, 15 (mars-avril 1900): 254-277.
tone_statements.quote: Dans tout le cours de cet article, on entend par accent uniquement l'accent d’intensité; cet accent est considéré comme étant entièrement indépendant du ton indo-européen, qui consistait en une élévation de la voix. ... dans tout mot à pénultième brève ..., l’accent frappait l’antépénultième et que la voyelle de la pénultième tombait. ... L’accent du persan n’est donc que le représentant actuel de l’accent attesté par la métrique gâthique; et cet accent lui-même répond à l’ictus du sanskrit dont la place est réglée par la quantité. Il semble ainsi qu’il soit légitime de reporter le point de départ de cet accent jusque dans la période indo-iranienne et sans doute jusqu’à l’indo-européen.
tone_statements.translation: Throughout this article, 'accent' means only the intensity accent; this accent is regarded as entirely independent of the Indo-European tone, which consisted in a raising of the voice. ... in every word with a short penult ..., the accent struck the antepenult and the vowel of the penult dropped. ... The accent of Persian is therefore only the present-day representative of the accent attested by Gathic metre; and that accent itself corresponds to the ictus of Sanskrit, whose place is regulated by quantity. It thus seems legitimate to carry the starting point of this accent back into the Indo-Iranian period and no doubt to Indo-European.
tone_statements.check: quotation verified in source (minor differences in wording)
tone_statements.summary: Stress (intensity) accent, quantity-regulated: antepenult if penult light, else penult; IE pitch 'ton' set aside as independent, not asserted for OP.

audit.reasoning: Both deciding quotations were found verbatim at the stated locators in copies we hold (Kent 1950 sec. 59(i) p. 25; Skjaervo 2016 p. 18). The classification 'undetermined' rests on the standard reference grammar of a dead corpus language whose script does not mark accent, and is independently confirmed by every other description opened: Schmitt 2004 sec. 3.4 (held), and Meillet 1915 sec. 173 / Meillet-Benveniste 1931 sec. 173 (downloaded now to. The record already correctly separates Kent's 'no evidence' from Skjaervo's hedged comparative conjecture (rightmost non-final heavy) and Schmitt's note that OP>MP final-syllable loss suggests a Latin-type fixed accent. No better source can exist in principle; the only improvement would be citing Skjaervo's conjecture from his 2009 Routledge chapter rather than the not-for-citation primer. Limitation: n

sources.quote: We do not know the rules for Old Persian stress, but some rules may be formulated from comparison with other Iranian languages and Indic. In words of two, three, or four syllables, the heavy syllable closest to the end of the word, not counting the last syllable, probably took the stress. Here “heavy syllable” = a syllable with a long vowel or a diphthong or a short vowel followed by more than one consonant (or an unwritten n or h + cons.) and “light syllable” = syllable with a short vowel followed by only one consonant: kā´ra, Višt´āspa, ām´ātā, Auramazd´āha, kāsakáina / vaz´ạrka, Auramázdā, Ariyārámna / fr´ābara, duvit´āparanam / mártiya, víspazanā [...] In words with several short syllables the stress moved toward the beginning of the word: bága, návama, but we do not know how far it was allowed to go and so, for instance, where the stress lay in hamaranakara and other words with four or more short syllables, e.g.: ákunavam or akúnavam, hámaranakara or hamáranakàra (à = secondary stress), úšhamaranakara or ušhamáranakara.
sources.note: Same work as the 2002 citation, in its 2016 revision (title page: 'An Introduction to Old Persian', 'Copyright (c) 2016 by Prods Oktor Skjaervo'; the catalog cite already names the 2016 primer). The section is explicitly conjectural: no rules are known; a rule is proposed from comparison with other Iranian and Indic. Proposed rule: in 2-4 syllable words the rightmost heavy syllable, excluding the final syllable, takes the stress; heavy = long vowel, diphthong, or short vowel + more than one consonant (or unwritten n/h + consonant); light = short vowel + one consonant. Final closed syllables: u

sources.quote: 'Une insuffisance commune aux inscriptions perses et au texte avestique ... : on n'y trouve rien qui puisse renseigner soit sur une conservation eventuelle du ton indo-iranien, soit sur la place d'un accent. ... Mais il est impossible de dire s'il subsistait des traces du ton, qu'il soit reste mobile comme en vedique, ou qu'il ait tendu a se fixer.'

tone.quote: Une insuffisance commune aux inscriptions perses et au texte avestique, comme d’ailleurs à toutes les inscriptions anciennes en langues indo-européennes : on n’y trouve rien qui puisse renseigner soit sur une conservation éventuelle du ton indo-iranien, soit sur la place d’un accent. Le rythme quantitatif de l’indo-iranien s’est mainienu en persan, en se combinant avec une influence de la fin de mot; on peut donc être sûr qu'il existait en perse. Mais 1l est impossible de dire s’il subsistait des traces du ton, qu'il soit resté mobile comme en védique, ou qu’il ait tendu à se fixer.
tone.locator: sec. 173, p. 101 ('Insuffisance des données', end of ch. II Phonétique)
tone.translation: A deficiency common to the Persian inscriptions and the Avestan text, as indeed to all ancient inscriptions in Indo-European languages: one finds nothing in them that could inform either about a possible preservation of the Indo-Iranian tone or about the place of an accent. The quantitative rhythm of Indo-Iranian was maintained in (modern) Persian, combining with an influence of the word end; one can therefore be sure it existed in Old Persian. But it is impossible to say whether traces of the tone survived, whether it stayed mobile as in Vedic, or whether it had tended to become fixed.
tone.says: Extinct language of the Achaemenid cuneiform inscriptions; the script records neither tone nor accent, and it is impossible to tell whether any trace of the inherited Indo-Iranian tone survived.

sources.citation: Meillet, Antoine. 1900. La déclinaison et l'accent d'intensité en perse. Journal Asiatique, 9e série, 15 (mars-avril 1900): 254-277.
sources.quote: Dans tout le cours de cet article, on entend par accent uniquement l'accent d’intensité; cet accent est considéré comme étant entièrement indépendant du ton indo-européen, qui consistait en une élévation de la voix. ... dans tout mot à pénultième brève ..., l’accent frappait l’antépénultième et que la voyelle de la pénultième tombait. ... L’accent du persan n’est donc que le représentant actuel de l’accent attesté par la métrique gâthique; et cet accent lui-même répond à l’ictus du sanskrit dont la place est réglée par la quantité. Il semble ainsi qu’il soit légitime de reporter le point de départ de cet accent jusque dans la période indo-iranienne et sans doute jusqu’à l’indo-européen.
sources.note: The accent operative in Old Persian was an accent d'intensité (stress), explicitly treated as independent of the Indo-European 'ton' (pitch, 'élévation de la voix'); its place was regulated by quantity: on the antepenult when the penult was short (the penult vowel then syncopated: visati > bīst, duvaisatai > duvēst), otherwise on the penult; long vowels attracted secondary accents; closing pages tie this quantity-regulated an earlier reading to Gathic metre and the Sanskrit an earlier reading and project it back to Indo-Iranian. Nothing is claimed about survival of lexical tone in Old Persian.

tone.quote: § 307. Zur Betonung. Die Betonung ist in beiden altiranischen Dialekten unbezeichnet geblieben. I. Für das Altpersische ist nichts zu ermitteln. II. Für das Awestische haben wir wenigstens einige Anhaltspunkte, die dafür zeugen, dass die Sprache im Wesentlichen auf dem arischen Betonungsstandpunkt verharrte, wenigstens noch zu der Zeit, da gewisse Lautveränderungen stattfanden. ... Die an sich wahrscheinliche Annahme, dass in Compositen bei der Vereinigung zusammenstossender Vocale sich der Schleifton einstellte, scheint mir ... eine gewisse Bestätigung zu erhalten.
tone.translation: § 307. On accentuation. Accentuation has remained unmarked in both Old Iranian dialects. I. For Old Persian nothing can be determined. II. For Avestan we have at least a few clues testifying that the language essentially remained at the Aryan (Indo-Iranian) stage of accentuation, at least at the time when certain sound changes took place. ... The inherently probable assumption that in compounds the slurred (circumflex) tone arose when colliding vowels merged seems to me ... to receive some confirmation.

tone.quote: the standard explanation for the loss of inflectional endings in Iranic languages like Persian is that it was simply a matter of the position of a strong stress accent. ... Note that the position of the stress accent is inferred by the loss of syllables, not the other way around. ... For all we know, the assignment of the stress accent to the received position was simultaneous with the loss of final syllables, not its cause. Ancient records do not otherwise indicate the position of the stress on Old Persian words, but we know that the accentual outcome was not inherited from Proto-Indo-Iranic.
